summary: Catalogs experiences from developing infrastructure for a national, multi-organizational directory service and piloting it with off-the-shelf directory products.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a lessons-learned report from building a nationwide people-lookup service.

subtitle: Lessons and insights from implementing a nationwide directory service with off-the-shelf software.

tldr.problem: Building and deploying a large-scale directory service that must work with multiple commercial software packages and real-world constraints is far more complex than the ideal specification suggests.
tldr.mechanism: The TISDAG project documented both successes (successful referral service, protocol mapping efficiency, reasonable response times) and surprises (LDAP schema limitations, index object compression issues, commercial software quirks).
tldr.outcome: The project demonstrated the feasibility of federated directory services but revealed that deployments need to account for real software limitations, performance considerations, and WDSP participation dynamics.

today: RFC 2969 is Informational and provides the project team's experience report from October 2000. The TISDAG project informed subsequent work in federated directory services and distributed directory system design. The lessons documented here remain relevant to modern distributed service architectures.

sections.title: The TISDAG Project and Its Goals
sections.content:
As described in RFC 2967, the TISDAG project set out to provide the infrastructure for a national Swedish whitepages directory service. The goal was to let end-users search for contact information across multiple providers without requiring those providers to replicate their data to a central location.

Two independent software implementations were created based on the TISDAG specification, and a pilot deployment was set up within the Swedish University Network (SUNET) to test the architecture against reality. This RFC captures the experiences of the implementation and deployment teams—both successes and surprises—to inform future directory service projects.

The authors emphasize that this document reflects their own observations and acknowledges that other project participants may have different experiences or insights. It is a record of what one team learned, not an exhaustive evaluation.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors built a real phone-lookup system based on the TISDAG design and are sharing what actually happened when they tried to make it work.

sections.title: Successes and Key Achievements
sections.content:
The pilot system demonstrated several important successes. The architecture worked as intended: the system successfully acted as middleware between client software and WDSP servers. Neither clients nor servers had to change significantly; the DAG looked like a server to clients and a client to servers.

The project achieved reasonable response times, typically providing answers within 10 seconds even with limited testbeds of 10 WDSPs. While not as fast as a direct query to a single provider, this met the project's goal of response times comparable to typical web-server access.

Protocol mapping efficiency was demonstrated. Instead of requiring N × M mappings (each of N client protocols to each of M WDSP protocols), the system achieved N + M complexity by mapping each protocol to the internal DAG/IP. The prototype system also showed success in mapping between different data schemas, partly because the DAG's schemas were deliberately kept simple and minimal.
sections.plainLanguage: The system worked nearly as designed: it sat between different kinds of software and translated between them without either side needing major changes. Queries came back in reasonable time. Translating between 5 protocols and 3 backend types was easier than expected.

sections.title: Challenges and Operational Realities
sections.content:
The RFC catalogs several surprises that surfaced during implementation and deployment. LDAP objectclass limitations: standard LDAP person objectclasses did not include the o (organization) attribute, even though TISDAG needed to search by organization. The standard assumption was that organization would be part of the distinguished name, making it difficult to handle people across multiple organizations.

Index object compression: the Tagged Index Object (TIO) format used to transmit provider summaries did not achieve the compression efficiency that simpler formats achieved. Long tag lists meant that as indexes grew, compression became less effective than initially expected. Reinflating indexes to perform joins on tags also added computational cost.

Status message mapping: when query chaining contacted multiple WDSPs, some inevitably returned errors or became unreachable. Deciding how to report this to the end-user was difficult—should the client think the query succeeded if some WDSPs answered? Most commercial client protocols lacked the sophistication to express this nuance.

Commercial software limitations: real-world LDAP and Whois++ clients had their own expectations, implementation quirks, and shortcuts. Some clients supported only a small subset of protocol error codes. Some automatically appended additional search terms to user queries. One LDAPv3 client could not handle referral responses (response code 10), making referrals useless in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: When the team tried to use standard software, they found many unexpected limits: missing database fields, poor compression, software that broke easily, and client programs that changed queries on their own.

sections.title: Performance Factors and Future Directions
sections.content:
The RFC documents several factors affecting system performance. Query type matters: substring searches are slower than exact matches because they must be sent to backend servers and generate more results to filter. The number of search attributes affects performance—too few generates many hits; too many slows the initial lookup. The number of directories matters: more directories mean more potential referrals and more data to process. Chained queries (where the DAG fetches results) are slower than referrals (where the client fetches), because results must pass through the DAG. Ultimately, the system is only as fast as the slowest backend WDSP server involved.

For future work, the RFC proposes several directions. Enhanced WDSP participation: the quality of index objects generated by WDSPs significantly affects system performance; there should be clearer guidelines or feedback when WDSPs generate poor indexes. Performance monitoring: WDSPs that are consistently slow should be identified and potentially encouraged to improve. Schema flexibility: future systems should support customized or domain-specific schemas to allow broader WDSP participation. Security: the pilot focused on public whitepages data; future work should add authentication, authorization, and encryption for sensitive information.

The RFC notes that the original TISDAG architecture, designed for the simple role of "find things that match and let the client decide," gradually evolved toward being a more sophisticated transparent protocol proxy. While this better served the national whitepages application, it raised questions about whether the architecture would remain flexible enough for other applications.
sections.plainLanguage: System speed depends on what type of search, how many databases are involved, and how fast each database responds. Future versions should have better quality control, security, and more flexible data formats.

viz.caption: Factors affecting DAG system query performance

items.title: Query type
items.text: Substring queries slower than exact; sent to all backends.

items.title: Number of attributes
items.text: Too few generates excessive hits; too many slows initial lookup.

items.title: Backend performance
items.text: Overall response time never faster than slowest WDSP.

items.title: Query chaining vs. referrals
items.text: Referrals faster because DAG does not process results; chaining requires full data processing.
